prompt: How does a torchvision transform used for augmentation differ from lesson 7's shifted copies?
hint: When is the change made, and is it kept?

choices.text: It changes the validation images too
choices.why: Validation is read as drawn in both approaches; augmentation is for training only.

choices.text: A new random change each time an image is used
choices.why: Right. Each epoch sees fresh variants, and the training set on disk stays the same size.

choices.text: It works only on photographs, not on 8 by 8 digits
choices.why: `augment.py` ran it on the digits as 1x8x8 tensors with no conversion.

choices.text: It writes every variant into a larger dataset before training
choices.why: That is what lesson 7 did; the transform does the opposite.

prompt: `shift(batch)` was called once on a batch of four digits. What did the output show?
hint: Compare the four drawings with each other.

choices.text: Each digit moved in its own direction
choices.why: That is what the per-image call produced, with `torch.stack`.

choices.text: The batch was refused with a shape error
choices.why: v2 transforms accept leading dimensions; the call ran.

choices.text: All four moved by the same shift
choices.why: Right. One call is one sample to v2, so one shift is drawn for the whole batch.

choices.text: Nothing moved, because the seed was fixed
choices.why: A fixed seed makes the draws repeatable, not zero.

prompt: A colleague augments with `x_aug = jitter(x[idx])` inside the training loop, where `x[idx]` is a batch of 32 images. What is the effect?
hint: How many draws does one call make?

choices.text: Each of the 32 images gets its own random turn and shift
choices.why: That needs one call per image; one call on the batch draws once.

choices.text: The whole batch moves as one, so the variety is far smaller
choices.why: Right. The fix is to call the transform per image, in `__getitem__` or with `torch.stack`.

choices.text: The labels are turned along with the images
choices.why: The labels are a separate tensor the call never sees.

choices.text: Training crashes on the first batch
choices.why: It runs without complaint, which is why this mistake survives.

prompt: What does an augmentation claim about the images it changes?
hint: Training uses the old label with the new image.

choices.text: That the label is still right after the change
choices.why: Right, and for a 6 turned upside down the claim is false.

choices.text: That the image becomes easier to classify
choices.why: Augmented images are usually harder; that is part of what they teach.

choices.text: That the validation set will contain such images
choices.why: It says nothing about validation, which is read as drawn.

choices.text: That the network has seen this exact change before
choices.why: The point is the opposite: a change it has not seen.

prompt: In `preserve.py`, how many of the validation 6s turned upside down did the network read as 9?
hint: The second-to-last line, the last count.

prompt: You classify chest X-rays where the heart sits on the patient's left. Which augmentation does the lesson's rule refuse?
hint: Which change would a radiologist notice as wrong?

choices.text: A shift of a few pixels
choices.why: Where the image is framed does not change the diagnosis.

choices.text: A small change of brightness
choices.why: Exposure varies between machines; a little of it keeps the label, unless the task is about density.

choices.text: A horizontal flip
choices.why: Right. It puts the heart on the right, an anatomy that is a finding of its own, under the old label.

choices.text: A turn of three degrees
choices.why: Patients are never perfectly straight; a small turn is a change the label survives.

prompt: In `augtrain.py`, which policy did the most damage, and why?
hint: Look at the last row and think of 6 and 9.

choices.text: Shift and turn, because the network saw too many variants
choices.why: It was the best row of the four.

choices.text: Mirror, because half the images were changed
choices.why: It did harm, but less than any turn.

choices.text: Any turn: 6s and 9s were taught as both
choices.why: Right, and every digit had to be learnt in every orientation from ten examples.

choices.text: None, because without augmentation it overfitted
choices.why: No augmentation scored above both unsafe policies.

prompt: Why does `augtrain.py` evaluate with `loop.evaluate` on the plain validation images?

choices.text: It measures the real images the model will meet
choices.why: Right. Augmenting it would score the model on images nobody will send it.

choices.text: Because `loop.evaluate` cannot take a transform
choices.why: It could be written to; the reason is what is measured, not the function.

choices.text: To make the comparison between policies faster
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; the plain set is the right thing to measure.

choices.text: Because augmented validation would always score higher
choices.why: It would usually score lower, and either way it measures the wrong images.

prompt: 25 of the 64 units before `base.pt`'s head stay at zero for every digit from 5 to 9. What does that tell you?
hint: Who shaped that layer, and for what?

choices.text: That layer fits 0 to 4; cut earlier for a new task
choices.why: Right. Keeping only the convolutions brought the score back up to 0.917 to 0.922.

choices.text: The units died because the learning rate was too high
choices.why: They fire for 0 to 4, which scored 0.989; they are silent only on the new digits.

choices.text: The new head needs more epochs to wake them
choices.why: The head sits after them and cannot change what they output; they are frozen.

choices.text: Nothing; a ReLU at zero is normal and harmless
choices.why: At zero for one image, yes. At zero for every new image, the feature is lost to the task.

prompt: You have 300 photographs of five kinds of machine part. Which start does the lesson suggest trying first?
hint: What made borrowing lose here, and would it apply?

choices.text: Train from scratch only, since transfer lost in every run of this lesson
choices.why: It lost because the donor was tiny; a large, broad donor changes that.

choices.text: A frozen ImageNet body with a new head, plus a from-scratch baseline
choices.why: Right. The donor is far larger than the task, and the baseline says whether it paid.

choices.text: Pretrain on the 300 photographs, then transfer to themselves
choices.why: A donor no larger than the task is exactly the case that failed.

choices.text: `base.pt`, since it is already trained
choices.why: It knows 8 by 8 grey digits, nothing about photographs of parts.

Why must images passed to an ImageNet body be normalised with `mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406]`?

choices.text: Because those are the means of your own images

choices.text: To turn colour photographs into grey ones
